catalog_quote: Many languages have stress or accent systems, which generally have at least a partially undulating, rhythmical nature (alternating stress rules, clash avoidance, etc.). Jamsay is a tone language, whose tones are important both lexically and grammatically. Unlike the case in other (non-Dogon) tone languages of the area, in Jamsay there is no “tone sandhi” across word boundaries. In native vocabulary, long words may consist entirely of metrically light, monomoraic Cv syllables. For these reasons, there is no phonetically obvious metrical structure of the sort we observe in English. However, an embryonic metrical structure is manifested in various phonological rules, particularly those applying to verb stems and their suffixal derivatives (including Verbal Nouns). The core sequence involved is a stem-initial bisyllabic [σσ] foot behaving metrically as a trochee [sw], i.e., with a metrically strong σ1 followed by a weak σ2. ... There is no clear evidence for metrical structure in the third, fourth, and fifth syllables of long, uncompounded stems or words. (ms p. 26) ... If the metrical structure were better developed, one would expect some kind of undulating stress, so that e.g. a five-syllable word would have an audible organization into metrical feet, e.g. [sw][sw]σ (with extra-metrical final syllable). This is not the case. (ms p. 28)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Jamsay word prosody is lexical and grammatical tone (mora = TBU); the grammar describes no word stress or accent. The only stress-like asymmetry is an abstract stem-initial trochaic foot (strong syllable 1, weak syllable 2) inferred from segmental lenition/syncope rules that target syllable 2, explicitly not an audible stress and not iterated through longer words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None; Heath explicitly says there is no undulating/alternating rhythm ([sw][sw]σ organization 'is not the case').
new_statements.exceptions: Nominal (crypto-)compounds of 4+ syllables show a slight impressionistic pitch drop on V2 (HHHL heard as HMHL) marking a compound juncture, 'a hint of trochaic meter' (sec. 3.2.3, p. 28); Fulfulde loans likewise. Heath flags these as impressionistic and needing instrumental study.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns word/stem-level prosody. Gerasimov 2025 (ThoT report, sec. 5.2 p. 9, second-hand from Heath 2008 + Heath p.c.) states flatly 'Jamsay has no stress' and 'There is no positional prominence in Jamsay'.
new_statements.identity_note: Heath's data are chiefly from the Douentza-area (mainly Dianwely) Jamsay; he notes a distinct Gourou dialect (Koro) and separate Pergue dialect notes exist, but the grammar describes mainstream Jamsay = jams1239. Quote is from the author's Jan-2008 pre-publication ms; Gerasimov 2025, working from the published Mouton edition, cites the same passage as Heath 2008: 26-28, so ms and book pagination coincide here.

tone_statements.quote: In Jamsay, the tonal requirements of the Mod head again dominate; however, unlike Tommo So, the tone of the possessor also surfaces as low. We analyze the difference between Tommo So and Jamsay as due to the prosodic target of the active tonal overlay constraints. For Tommo So, leftward docking of the modifier's L tone targets a prosodic word (the noun), whereas in Jamsay it targets a prosodic phrase (Poss + Noun).

tone_statements.summary: In possessor-noun-adjective phrases the adjective's L overlay covers both the noun and the possessor in Jamsay, i.e. the whole preceding prosodic phrase. Secondary data (McPherson 2014; McPherson & Heath 2016); consistent with the catalog's Heath 2008 tone entry.

tone_statements.summary: Jamsay's genitive linker mà blocks the possessor-controlled overlay, unlike Tommo So and Yanda Dom; in recursive possession each possessor imposes {HL} on the next noun and a final demonstrative casts {L} over the whole string. Numeral túrú 'one' is inert except in 'one of his hands', where it lowers the noun.

sources.note: Sec. 3.2.2 'Embryonic metrical structure' (pp. 26-28): Jamsay is a tone language; 'there is no phonetically obvious metrical structure'; only an 'embryonic' stem-initial trochaic [sw] foot visible in segmental lenition rules targeting syllable 2; no undulating stress in long words ('This is not the case'). Sec. 2.1: tone and intonation central. No word-stress rule anywhere in the grammar (a full-text search for stress/accent: stress/accent occur only in this section and in non-prosodic senses).

sources.note: Dogon NP tonosyntax (word-level tone overlays triggered by modifiers/possessors) arose from the interlocking of (a) a right-headed prosodic pattern in noun-modifier sequences, (b) loss of numeral classifiers that had shielded nouns before numerals, and (c) transfer of tones from possessors to following possessums; the accidental system was reinterpreted semantically and is stable.
